```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Oracle REST Data Services (ORDS) exposes selected Oracle tables and
database procedures through web APIs. Use it when your Shiny app needs to
read Oracle data over HTTPS without installing Oracle client libraries.

`oauth_db_oracle_ords_api()` reads collections of records and calls custom
JSON endpoints with each visitor's access token. ORDS controls access to
those endpoints; the database and endpoint code determine which data they
return. For SQL queries through DBI or dbplyr, use the separate
[Oracle Database guide](oracle.html).

## Set up ORDS and sign-in

Ask your administrator for an HTTPS ORDS endpoint exposing the resources
your app needs. The example reads an AutoREST collection, which exposes
table records as JSON. Use the schema alias URL, including any reverse-proxy
prefix, and replace `orders` with your collection's name.

ORDS must protect the resource and accept JWT access tokens from your
sign-in provider. External-provider JWT profiles require ORDS 23.3 or
later; see the [ORDS authentication guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-rest-data-services/26.3/orddg/developing-REST-applications.html)
for issuer, audience and privilege mappings.

Register your Shiny app with that provider, using `http://localhost:8100`
as the redirect URI. Request the access scope for the resource and enable
refresh tokens if you use `offline_access`. Save the settings in
`.Renviron` and restart R:

```text
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-shiny-app-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-shiny-app-client-secret
OAUTHDB_ORDS_ISSUER=https://login.example.org/realms/reporting
OAUTHDB_ORDS_SCOPE=reports.read
OAUTHDB_ORDS_URL=https://data.example.org/ords/reporting
```

## A complete app

```{r app}
library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

scope <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORDS_SCOPE")
provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORDS_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "offline_access", scope),
  required_scopes = scope
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    verbatimTextOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  ords <- oauth_db_oracle_ords_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORDS_URL"),
    required_scopes = scope
  )
  output$rows <- renderPrint({
    ords$select("orders", query = list(limit = 20L))$items
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)
```

Save this as `example.R`, run `source("example.R")`, and open
`http://localhost:8100` in a regular browser. Sign in to read one page of
the collection. Results are JSON lists, with records in `items`. Use
`offset` and `limit` to fetch further pages; the client doesn't follow
pagination links automatically.

For a custom JSON handler, call its relative path:

```{r custom-handler}
result <- ords$request(
  c("api", "sales"),
  query = list(country = "NL"),
  trailing_slash = TRUE
)
```

`select()` handles AutoREST collection paths. For a custom endpoint,
`request()` uses the path you supply; set `trailing_slash = TRUE` if it
needs one. See `?oauth_db_oracle_ords_api` for other request methods and
raw responses.

## User identity and data access

ORDS validates the JWT and enforces its resource privileges. The JWT subject
is available to handlers as `:current_user`. An ORDS role is not automatically
an Oracle database role, and accepting a user JWT does not by itself change
the database schema used by a handler. Configure handler filtering or a
supported end-user security context to enforce the required per-user data
access. Verify two users with different permissions before deployment.

Each call uses a current token and discards results after sign-out or
account changes. Read requests can refresh and retry once after HTTP 401;
writes don't retry automatically. The client returns your custom handler's
JSON without interpreting application-specific status fields.
